reading.rtitle: Your First International Congress: A Networking Guide
paras: Many nurses go to an international congress for the talks. But experienced professionals know a secret: the most important part of the congress often happens during the coffee breaks. That is where networking happens.

First, wear your name badge where people can see it. It shows your name, your hospital and your country, and it is the easiest icebreaker in the room. Then, do not stay with your own team all the time. Mingle. Walk around, visit the company booths, and talk to people you do not know.

To start a conversation, use polite questions. Instead of a direct question like 'Where is the keynote?', try 'Do you know where the keynote is?' or 'Could you tell me which session you are going to?' They sound friendlier, and people are happy to answer. Small talk is fine at the start: the city, the coffee, the last talk you saw.

Finally, when the conversation goes well, exchange contacts. Many people now use a QR code on their phone instead of a business card. And do not forget the most important step: reach out within a week, with a short message. A contact you never write to is not really a contact. If you keep in touch, one coffee break can open doors for years.

items.situation: You cannot find the main hall. Ask someone politely.
tips: Excuse me, do you know where the main hall is?
Do you know where + subject + verb.

items.situation: You want to know what time the keynote starts. Ask the person next to you.
tips: Could you tell me what time the keynote starts?
No do/does inside the indirect question.

items.situation: You think the person works with robotic surgery. Ask politely.
tips: I was wondering if you work with robotic surgery too.

tips: Do you know where the booth is?

items.situation: The conversation went well. End it and exchange contacts.
tips: It was great to meet you. Could we exchange contacts and keep in touch?
Exchange contacts, then promise to reach out.

listenings.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the International Robotic Surgery Congress here in Orlando. Before we start, a few quick notes. The keynote begins at nine thirty in the main hall, so please take your seats a few minutes before. Coffee breaks are at ten forty-five and at three fifteen, in the exhibition area, where you can also visit the company booths. Please wear your name badge at all times. You need it to enter every session. On Thursday evening, there is a networking reception on the terrace from six to eight. It is a great chance to mingle and meet colleagues from more than forty countries. If you have any questions, the help desk is next to the main entrance. Enjoy the congress.

Hi Doctor Chen, this is Andreia Heins, the nurse from Einstein Hospital in Sao Paulo. We met at the coffee break on Thursday, near the Medtronic booth, and we talked about training programs for robotic surgery nurses. I just wanted to say it was a pleasure to meet you. I was wondering if you could send me the article about your simulation program. And do you know if your team is coming to the Latin American meeting in March? It would be great to see you there. I will send you an email today with my contact details, so we can keep in touch. Thank you, and have a good week.

extra_audio.text: Here is how Andreia networks at the congress. First, she puts on her name badge and goes to the coffee break. Then she starts a conversation with an icebreaker about the keynote. Next, she asks polite indirect questions about the other person's work. After that, she exchanges contacts with a QR code. Finally, she reaches out with a short message the next week.
